text:
The Defense Health Agency will release full TRICARE cost updates for 2027 in time for next month’s Open Season, but new costs for premium-based plans already are available.

Here’s what beneficiaries will pay in the coming year for TRICARE Retired Reserve, TRICARE Reserve Select, TRICARE Young Adult, and the Continued Health Care Benefit Program, along with links to more details about these plan types. For more information on TRICARE coverage overall, check out MOAA’s TRICARE Guide.

TRICARE Retired Reserve

What: Coverage open to retired reservists under age 60, their families, and their survivors.

Learn More: Tricare Retired Reserve

2026 Monthly Premiums: $645.90 (member only), $1,548 (family)

2027 Monthly Premiums: $707.59 (member only), $1,697.70 (family)

TRICARE Reserve Select

What: Coverage open to Selected Reserve members and their family members. Individual Ready Reserve members are not eligible. Members are not eligible if they are on active duty orders for more than 30 days.

Learn More: TRICARE Reserve Select

2026 Monthly Premiums: $57.88 (member only), $286.66 (family)

2027 Monthly Premiums: $60.54 (member only), $307.48 (family)

TRICARE Young Adult

What: Coverage for unmarried adult children (ages 21 to 26) who aren’t eligible for an employer-sponsored plan or other TRICARE coverage. Children enrolled in full-time study can remain under other TRICARE coverage until age 23.

Learn More: TRICARE Young Adult

2026 Monthly Premiums: $363 (Select), $794 (Prime)

2027 Monthly Premiums: $394 (Select), $893 (Prime)

Continued Health Care Benefit Program (CHCBP)

What: Temporary coverage (18 to 36 months) for beneficiaries who lose TRICARE eligibility. Plan mirrors TRICARE Select, including prescription coverage.

Learn More: CHCBP (Humana Military)

2026 Monthly Premiums: $2,103 (single), $5,339 (family)

2027 Monthly Premiums: $2,280 (single), $5,741 (family)

Catastrophic Caps

All of the above plans, along with other TRICARE offerings, have a catastrophic cap – a maximum amount a beneficiary pays for covered care in a calendar year. Premiums do not count toward the cap and must continue to be paid even if the cap is reached during the year.

title: JBER opens direct-access clinic for women experiencing menopause symptoms - Your Alaska Link
description: JBER has opened a women’s mid-life clinic offering lab testing, hormone therapy and education for eligible TRICARE beneficiaries experiencing perimenopause and menopause.
text:
A new clinic at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson is expanding healthcare options for women experiencing perimenopause and menopause.
The 673rd Medical Group recently opened the Women’s Mid-Life Optimizations Direct Access Clinic, offering services such as diagnostic lab testing and hormone therapy to help patients manage symptoms linked to hormonal changes.
The clinic is available to eligible TRICARE beneficiaries and does not require a referral.
Patients can start the screening process by visiting or calling the Women’s Health Clinic. After an initial screening and lab testing, eligible patients will be contacted about two weeks later to schedule an in-person appointment.
Patients will also attend an educational session covering menopause, perimenopause and available treatments.
The clinic is located on the first floor of the JBER hospital’s Women’s Health Center, near the emergency room in the Moose Area.
For more information or to begin screening, call 907-580-5808.

I heard this so many times.

Commanders, NCOS, 30+ year vets who were on lifetime Tricare. Every time I thought to myself, “99% of Americans seem to be figuring it out... what am I missing?”

It turns out not much. (And if you want to hear more, check out our transition 101 webinar Nov 4 at Sitreps dot com / webinars. Stephen Spake, my former platoon sergeant turned health care guru will be diving into this)

Don’t get me wrong, healthcare coverage and affordability in the US can and should improve (I’ll leave the debate on how for another thread, maybe on X lol).

But... 82% of Americans at present report that they are overall satisfied with their healthcare coverage. Which contrasts sharply with the hellscape that commanders and field grades claimed I would walk into should I decide to leave.

So, what are realistic costs?

That depends on a few things. If you’re in the reserves or National Guard your Tricare premiums are roughly $280/ month for your entire family. If you’re 100% disabled, your family has champva capped at $3K/year.

The average employee with a family of four will pay roughly $9-$12K total per year in the US. About $7K of that monthly premiums and the rest out of pocket deductibles and uncovered costs.

Is that worse than free? Yeah, sure. But for most people getting out they should ask if they’d stay in if branch called and offered a $10K per year bonus. I think we all know instinctively what that answer would be.

title: After a crash, can blood reach you in time? | Health | wyomingnews.com
description: ImageTrend reports that receiving blood before reaching a hospital is far from universally available.
text:
Alicia Raebel was grocery shopping with her three sons when a crash-alert service called. Her husband, John Mazanec, had been in a motorcycle wreck. He was not answering his phone.
After a truck turned across his path in Pueblo, Colorado, on Sept. 4, 2025, paramedics found him bleeding heavily. Another crew brought blood from the ambulance company's base, and his transfusion began on the way to the hospital. The local program had launched just eight days earlier, according to
an August 2026 account published by UCHealth
.

"Had they not started me on the blood, I don't think I would be here," Mazanec told UCHealth.
Mazanec's case is one example of a treatment occurring across the country. Drawing on a representative sample of U.S. EMS incidents,
ImageTrend's
2026 EMS Insights Report
documented 1,695 crash patients receiving blood before hospital arrival in 2025. Those cases offer a broader picture of how blood reaches patients.
But receiving blood before reaching a hospital is far from universally available.
America's Blood Centers
, an association representing independent blood centers, estimates that only 1% to 2% of EMS agencies nationwide carry blood.
Starting Jan. 1, 2027,
TRICARE
, the health program for service members, retirees and their families, will test whether paying ambulance providers separately for blood products and transfusion services improves access and patient outcomes for eligible beneficiaries.
Who receives blood before reaching the hospital
Across the report's blood-treatment records, 80% of responses involved trauma, 44% of recipients were ages 20 to 49 and 68% were recorded as male. Nearly 2 in 5 recipients were injured in traffic or motorcycle crashes.
ImageTrend, Source: ImageTrend 2026 EMS Insights Report, page 15.
For a severely injured patient, waiting until hospital arrival can mean continuing to lose blood during the ride. Uncontrolled bleeding from traumatic injuries is a leading cause of preventable death, according to the
American College of Surgeons
, and a significant loss can become fatal within minutes.
Giving blood before hospital arrival, called prehospital blood transfusion, allows responders to begin replacing what a patient has lost. A
2025 clinical practice guideline
from the Prehospital Blood Transfusion Coalition supports early transfusion for patients in hemorrhagic shock, when blood loss leaves the body unable to maintain adequate circulation.
Blood is not needed for every crash injury. Clinicians select patients using medical protocols, and a transfusion cannot replace bleeding control or surgery to repair internal injuries.
How blood reaches patients depends on the local response
According to the EMS Insights Report, in 2025, air units performed 87% of the report's documented blood administrations, while ground units performed 10%. These figures include emergencies beyond crashes.
Across the blood-treatment records, 42% of responses occurred in rural counties. Ground-unit transfusions were more concentrated in urban counties, where 77% took place.
In the report's motor-vehicle-crash analysis, blood was recorded in 0.67% of rural EMS activations, compared with 0.08% in metro areas.
For someone injured on a road outside town, or on a city street, those findings raise a practical question: Which crew could bring blood to the scene or administer it during the trip to a hospital?
An emergency blood program does not require every ambulance to carry blood. The
federal Office of EMS
describes regional programs in which 911 centers can dispatch blood resources to an emergency. One crew can bring blood to another already treating a patient, as happened in Mazanec's case.
That means the estimate that only 1% to 2% of EMS agencies carry blood tells just part of the story. A crew that doesn't stock blood may still be able to get it from another responding unit. Counting agencies alone cannot show which communities have access or how quickly blood can reach a patient.
The cost of keeping blood ready for the next emergency
A donated unit of blood needs a system to collect it, prepare it and make it available for treatment. America's Blood Centers says blood product
costs can run $500 to $925 or more per unit
. The association argues that bundled ambulance payments do not adequately cover those costs.
Ambulance programs also need temperature-monitored coolers, equipment to warm blood for transfusion and trained clinicians. Arrangements with blood suppliers and hospitals must cover replenishment and unused products. Keeping that service ready creates expenses even between emergencies.
A payment pilot will test a way to expand access
The
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services
moved transfusions into a higher ground-ambulance payment category in 2025, but blood remains bundled into the transport payment.
Under
a federal notice published in July
, TRICARE providers will be able to bill separately for medically necessary blood products and transfusion services during qualifying transports for eligible beneficiaries. The five-year pilot runs through Dec. 31, 2031, and will assess access, outcomes and costs.
Communities are exploring new ways to deliver blood
In Florida, a new demonstration explores delivery by air without an ambulance helicopter. On Oct. 1, 2026, Hillsborough County Fire Rescue
demonstrated a drone blood-delivery program
intended to bring a temperature-controlled unit of whole blood directly to an emergency scene at a paramedic's request.
The initial service is planned for two areas of unincorporated Hillsborough County covering 70 square miles. The department projects three and a half minutes or less from request to blood administration. That is a performance target, rather than a reported result from patient care.
The county's October announcement said live operations were expected in the coming weeks, with the first year serving as a proof of concept.
By tackling delivery times and financing, the drone program and reimbursement pilot address different parts of the same life-or-death problem: getting blood to a patient while it can still save them.
Residents can help before the next emergency
A useful question for your local EMS agency is whether blood can reach a severely bleeding patient before hospital arrival. Ask how it gets there and how the service is supported. That opens a more useful conversation than asking only whether one ambulance carries blood.
Blood donation supports the supply that hospitals and ambulance programs depend on.
Contact a local blood center about eligibility and appointments
. The federal Office of EMS identifies blood-bank partnerships and community blood drives as ways to support programs.
Residents can also learn bleeding control through the American College of Surgeons'
Stop the Bleed training
, which teaches direct pressure, wound packing and appropriate tourniquet use. If you encounter a crash, protect your own safety, call 911 and follow dispatcher instructions.
Mazanec underwent surgeries and rehabilitation. By summer 2026, he was fishing again with his wife and sons, UCHealth reported.
The transfusion was an early step in a long recovery. Making that step possible for another family requires blood donors, trained responders and a way to sustain the service before the next emergency begins.
About the research
ImageTrend used Collaborate data, an opt-in
nationally representative dataset of de-identified EMS records
from more than 3,100 organizations. The
2026 EMS Insights Report
identifies blood treatment through procedure and medication records, however, documentation practices may vary by agency.
This story was produced by
ImageTrend
and reviewed and distributed by
Stacker
.

text:
Nothing in the Department of Justice’s $1.8 billion health care fraud takedown in Los Angeles stops at the United States border. One of the defendants in the sweep announced on Thursday, October 22, is a Filipino American nurse accused of spending part of a $906 million Medicare and Tricare scheme on a beach resort in Cagayan province.

The photograph shows the Edward R. Roybal Federal Building and US Courthouse in downtown Los Angeles, where the federal cases were announced. It was taken in April 2022 and does not depict the takedown, any defendant or any beneficiary. (Photo: Busition, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0)

Marizel Yukee, a nurse practitioner from Nevada, was indicted in June in the Southern District of Texas. Prosecutors say she owned and ran four wound care companies in Texas, Nevada, California and Hawaii and billed for skin graft procedures that were never needed.

This story is about the wider sweep announced on October 22. It does not report any new charge against Yukee.

Her case is not part of the 15 defendants announced this week. It is the same federal campaign, run through the same Justice Department fraud division, and it is the part of the crackdown with a Philippine asset attached.

What prosecutors say Yukee did

According to the indictment filed on June 18 in Houston, Yukee and unnamed accomplices submitted about $906 million in claims to Medicare and Tricare between October 2023 and April 2025.

The claims were for allografts, tissue transplants that prosecutors describe as medically unnecessary. The filing says Yukee billed an average of more than $1 million per patient and that the government paid out about $297 million.

Prosecutors say she ignored Medicare’s rule on reporting the true invoice price of the grafts and instead billed far higher amounts. An email quoted in the indictment reportedly shows her telling colleagues to inflate prices.

Two companies acting as allograft distributors allegedly paid her nearly $16 million in kickbacks to push their products, and the indictment describes a network of referral and purchasing payments around the wound care businesses.

The Philippine property and the seizure

Federal prosecutors say part of the money went into a lifestyle that includes a multi-million dollar home in Hawaii, a Bulgari necklace valued at $865,000, a Ferrari worth $594,000, and the development of a $4.6 million resort in Santa Ana, Cagayan.

The US government has since seized $30 million in bank accounts, luxury cars and jewelry valued at nearly $2 million, the Department of Justice announced in June.

Item Detail per the Department of Justice Defendant Marizel Yukee, nurse practitioner, Nevada Where charged Southern District of Texas, Houston, indictment filed June 18, 2026 Claims submitted About $906 million to Medicare and Tricare, October 2023 to April 2025 Government payout About $297 million Alleged kickbacks received Nearly $16 million from two allograft distributors Assets seized $30 million in accounts, cars and jewelry worth nearly $2 million Philippine asset named $4.6 million beach resort in Santa Ana, Cagayan

Why it landed in the same week as the bigger sweep

The October 22 announcement in Los Angeles covered 15 defendants, including six medical professionals, and about $1.8 billion in allegedly fraudulent claims. Eight people were arrested that day.

The largest piece is a $1.6 billion scheme that prosecutors say trafficked vulnerable people across the country for sham substance abuse treatment. Another case charges an Anaheim heart surgeon and a Tarzana chiropractor over about $135 million in unnecessary artery procedures.

Justice Department officials framed the round as part of a wider push against benefits fraud, citing a $25 million whistleblower program announced by President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance two days earlier. The department says its health care fraud strike forces have charged more than 6,200 defendants since 2007.

The Los Angeles Times reported that California Attorney General Rob Bonta and First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli held competing news conferences the same morning, each claiming credit for the arrests. Bonta said state investigators made the arrest of the Anaheim surgeon.

What this means for Filipino families

For readers in the Philippines, the Cagayan resort is the detail that makes this a local story. A criminal judgment from a Texas court can, in principle, reach property acquired with proceeds traced to the fraud, including property abroad, though no Philippine court has been asked to act in this case and no forfeiture of the resort has been reported.

The practical warning is about recruitment, not prosecution. Prosecutors say both Yukee’s alleged scheme and the hospice cases in Los Angeles worked through the same door: trusted intermediaries signing up elderly patients for services they did not need and often did not understand.

Filipino Americans are a large share of the US health care workforce. Earlier this month, this desk reported on Filipino nurses who won a $1.85 million US settlement over quit-fee contracts, and on a bill that would fine H-1B employers up to $250,000 for visa fraud.

What is not established

An indictment is an allegation. Yukee is presumed innocent, and none of the charges described here has been proved in court.

No source reviewed for this article shows a conviction, a sentence or a plea from Yukee in this case. The seizure announced in June is a court-authorised asset hold, not a finding of guilt.

No Philippine court filing, forfeiture order or agency action concerning the Santa Ana resort appears in any source reviewed. The $906 million figure is the amount allegedly billed, not an amount collected.
